title: One Agent or Many? How to Choose Your AI Team
subtitle: A beginner's guide to picking agentic design patterns on Vertex AI
intro: You asked an AI to book a trip and it tried to do flights, hotels, and visas all at once — and got confused. Would you hire one super-assistant or a team of specialists?
takeaway: Pick the simplest agent pattern that meets your task: one agent for simple goals, many for complex ones, and always weigh speed, cost, and human oversight.

sections.heading: Analogy: One chef or a whole kitchen?
sections.body: Think of an agent as a cook who can decide steps and use tools to finish a goal. A design pattern is the kitchen layout: one all-in-one chef, or a team where one chops, one grills, and one plates. One chef is fast and cheap. A team handles complex orders but needs more coordination.

sections.heading: Why does this exist? Choosing the right team
sections.body: Agents are for open-ended, multi-step goals where the AI must decide what to do next using outside data. Use a single-agent pattern when the goal is simple with just a few tools — it is low cost and low waiting time. Use a multi-agent pattern when a complex workflow is better split among specialists who talk to each other. Choose based on complexity, latency vs accuracy, cost of inference calls, and need for human-in-the-loop oversight.

sections.heading: What can go wrong? When more agents make it worse
sections.body: Every extra agent adds inference calls — each time you pay the model to think — so cost and latency, or waiting time, go up. More agents can improve accuracy, or getting the right answer, but can also miscommunicate and loop. For high-stakes tasks like medical or money decisions, you need human-in-the-loop, where a person approves actions. So start simple and add agents only when proven needed.

steps.narration: Start with your goal and how complex it is.
Pick single vs multi-agent pattern based on requirements.
Use one agent for simple workflows to save time and money.
Use many agents for complex multi-step workflows.
Check latency vs accuracy and cost of inference calls.
Add human oversight for high-stakes decisions.

quiz.q: When is a single-agent pattern the better choice?
options: When the task is open-ended but simple with few tools
When you need 5 specialists to debate every answer
When latency doesn't matter at all
When you want the highest possible cost
quiz.why: Single-agent is fast, cheap, and works for straightforward goals; multi-agent is for complex workflows.

quiz.q: What can go wrong if you use too many agents and usage grows 100x?
options: Latency and inference cost explode first
The model becomes free to run
Human oversight is no longer needed
quiz.why: Each agent adds inference calls, so cost and wait time scale quickly and coordination can fail.

options: A person reviews or approves high-stakes agent actions
The AI trains a human to be faster
Agents only talk to other agents
quiz.why: It's required oversight for risky tasks to catch errors before they cause harm.
